mainTopic: Pebbles and tail-swinging, the chicken and the string, and what counts as normal eating (שן)
overview: This amud covers several topics in animal damages. First, the גמרא finishes a debate about pebbles kicked by an animal (צרורות). It asks whether רבי יוחנן's rule that חצי נזק is paid in every domain covers the public domain, and answers either that רבי זירא retracts or that רבי יוחנן meant only קרן. Next, two sages ask about an animal that does damage by swinging its tail. The answer is that this is normal behavior, unless the swinging is excessive. רב עינא's question about an animal swinging its organ ends in תיקו. The גמרא then explains the משנה about a string on a chicken's leg. It concludes that the משנה is a case where the chicken flung the string. It also shows that רב הונא's rule about an ownerless string tied by a person is a rolling בור. A new משנה on שן teaches that an animal eating food fit for it pays full damage in the damaged person's property. In the public domain the owner pays only for the benefit, and the משנה uses examples from the square and the store. The גמרא's discussion of that משנה explains what counts as normal eating, including רב פפא's cat and dates and רב יהודה's case of the donkey, the bread and the basket.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן's rule that half-damage is paid in every domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's rule that half-damage is paid in both private and public domains, and suggests it covers pebbles kicked and landing in the public domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוחנן said that half-damage is the same everywhere: it is paid in the private domain and in the public domain. Doesn't that include a case where the animal kicked pebbles in the public domain and they did damage in the public domain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that an animal is exempt when it kicks pebbles in the public domain and they cause damage there. It quotes רבי יוחנן, who says half-damage is paid no matter which domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage from kicked pebbles (צרורות) is paid as half-damage. רבי יוחנן says half-damage does not depend on the domain. The challenger reads this as covering even a case that happens entirely in the public domain, which would make the owner liable there too.

keyTerms.meaning: Half-damage: paying half of the loss
She (the animal) propelled or kicked up pebbles
"Isn't it that...?": the גמרא proposes a reading in order to challenge

phrases.english: But doesn't Rabbi Yoḥanan say:
Half-damage is not divided
phrases.notes: He means the half-damage payment works the same way in both places; neither place gives an exemption.

phrases.english: neither for the private domain
nor for the public domain.
What, is it not where it propelled pebbles in the public domain
and caused damage in the public domain?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens this section by challenging a ruling made before it on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that kicked pebbles in the public domain bring no payment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן says half-damage is paid in every domain. Read broadly, that includes a case that happens entirely in the public domain.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן meant pebbles that landed on private property
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רבי יוחנן's case is pebbles kicked in the public domain that did damage in a private domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. רבי יוחנן was talking about an animal that kicked pebbles in the public domain, and they did damage in a private domain.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers by narrowing רבי יוחנן's case. The damage happened on private property, not in the public domain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the damage landed in a private domain, the owner can be liable even though the kick started in public. So רבי יוחנן's rule no longer proves anything about damage done entirely in the public domain.

phrases.english: No; where it propelled pebbles in the public domain,
and caused damage in the private domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1 by limiting רבי יוחנן's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן's rule covers damage done entirely in the public domain.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן's rule covers pebbles kicked in public that damage in a private domain.

steps.title: But you yourself said the starting place is what counts
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא is challenged with his own earlier statement: only the starting point of the pebbles matters, not where they land.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said: if there is no 'lifting' here, is there 'placing' here? In other words, where the pebbles land does not matter.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה challenges רבי זירא's answer by quoting something רבי זירא himself said earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי זירא had said that what counts is where the pebbles started moving (the עקירה), not where they came down (the הנחה). If so, pebbles kicked in the public domain should be exempt even when they land on private property. That contradicts the answer he just gave.

keyTerms.meaning: Lifting up or uprooting: here, where the pebbles start moving
Placing or setting down: here, where the pebbles land
But you said: quoting the speaker's own earlier words against him

phrases.english: But didn't you say: There is no lifting here,
is there placing here?!
phrases.notes: He means: the kick started in the public domain, so the landing place can't create liability on its own.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמְרַתְּ: עֲקִירָה אֵין כָּאן, הַנָּחָה יֵשׁ כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's answer that the case is damage in a private domain
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By רבי זירא's own rule, only the starting point counts. A kick in the public domain should then be exempt wherever the pebbles land.

steps.title: רבי זירא takes back his earlier view
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא admits the contradiction and retracts his earlier statement.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I take back what I said.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers simply: he changes his mind about his earlier statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once he drops the rule that only the starting point counts, the answer in step 2 stands. Pebbles kicked in public that land in a private domain can bring liability.

keyTerms.meaning: I retract: I take back my words

phrases.english: He said to him: I retract.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the starting point of the pebbles matters.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי זירא withdraws that rule, so the answer in step 2 holds.

steps.title: Or: רבי יוחנן was speaking only about goring
steps.stepSummary: A second way out: רבי יוחנן's rule about half-damage in every domain refers to קרן, not to kicked pebbles.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say this: when רבי יוחנן gave his rule, he was talking about goring (קרן).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second answer. רבי זירא does not need to retract, because רבי יוחנן's rule was never about pebbles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Goring (קרן) is paid in the public domain as well, so 'half-damage in every domain' fits it well. Pebbles (צרורות) kicked in the public domain can then stay exempt, and רבי זירא's earlier rule about the starting point survives.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
Horn: the damage category of goring and other unusual, harmful acts

steps.whatToRemember: There are two answers to the contradiction. Either רבי זירא retracts, or רבי יוחנן's rule about paying in every domain applies only to קרן, not to kicked pebbles.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יוחנן's rule is cancelled here. In this second answer it still holds, just for קרן rather than for צרורות.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
When Rabbi Yoḥanan said it, it was about Goring.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כִּי אֲמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן – אֲקַרַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer, given instead of the retraction in step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן's rule covers kicked pebbles.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן's rule covers only קרן, so pebbles kicked in the public domain can stay exempt.

steps.title: Two sages ask about an animal swinging its tail
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה נשיאה and רבי אושעיא raise a new question: what is the law if an animal causes damage by swinging its tail?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה נשיאה and רבי אושעיא were sitting in רבי יהודה's entrance hall, and a question came up between them: if an animal swung its tail and caused damage, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a short story. It sets up a question about damage from tail-swinging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is which category tail-swinging belongs to. Is it like normal walking behavior, or like unusual harmful behavior such as goring? The answer to that decides whether the owner pays.

keyTerms.meaning: Entrance hall or front room of a house
A matter came up between them
She swung or wagged her tail

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה וְרַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and Rabbi Oshaya were sitting
in the entrance hall of Rabbi Yehuda,
a matter emerged from among them:
If it swung its tail, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה וְרַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion that does not depend on the pebbles debate.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the owner is liable when the animal causes damage by swinging its tail

steps.title: Should the owner hold its tail while walking?
steps.stepSummary: The other sage answers that swinging the tail is normal, so the owner cannot be expected to stop it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other one said to him: Should the owner hold onto its tail and walk along?!
steps.whatsHappening: The second sage answers with a rhetorical question. No owner can be expected to hold an animal's tail all the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Swinging the tail is something an animal does all the time. An owner can't reasonably prevent it, so he is not held responsible for this damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Must he hold onto it?: a rhetorical question

phrases.english: The other one said to him:
Must he grasp it by its tail and walk?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִידַּךְ: וְכִי יֹאחֲזֶנָּה בִּזְנָבָהּ וְיֵלֵךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner is not liable, because he can't be expected to control the tail.

steps.title: By that logic, goring would be exempt too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer: the same reasoning would exempt goring, yet we know the owner pays for קרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, say the same about goring: should the owner hold onto its horn and walk along?! But the owner does pay for goring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the answer from step 7 by applying it to goring. That would lead to a wrong result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner can't hold the horn all the time either, yet he pays for damage from קרן. So 'he can't hold it' cannot by itself be the reason for exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a challenge from the logic just stated

phrases.english: If so, regarding Goring too, let us say:
Must he grasp it by its horn and walk?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning that the owner can't be expected to hold the tail
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reasoning would exempt קרן, but קרן is liable.

steps.title: Goring is unusual; tail-swinging is normal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. Goring is not the animal's normal way, while swinging its tail is.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? Goring is not the animal's normal way, but this, swinging its tail, is its normal way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the challenge from step 8 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner must watch out for unusual harmful behavior like goring. He is not expected to stop an animal's ordinary, constant behavior like swinging its tail. So the answer in step 7 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare?: rejects a comparison

steps.whatToRemember: Liability depends on whether the behavior is the animal's normal way. Unusual acts like goring make the owner responsible. Ordinary acts like swinging the tail do not.

phrases.english: How can these be compared?!
Goring is not its typical way,
this is its typical way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge in step 8 and keeps the answer from step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between tail-swinging and goring
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Goring is unusual behavior an owner must guard against. Tail-swinging is normal behavior.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Damage from swinging the tail is treated as the animal's normal behavior, and the owner is not held responsible for it the way he is for goring.

steps.title: If tail-swinging is normal, what was the question?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the question from Step 6. If swinging the tail is normal behavior, the answer seems obvious, so why ask?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since swinging the tail is its normal way, what was he asking?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the original question of רבי יהודה נשיאה and רבי אושעיא. If swinging the tail is clearly normal, the question seems pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 9 the גמרא said tail-swinging is normal behavior. Normal behavior in the public domain brings no liability. So the answer is obvious, and the question looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: He was asking; it was a question for him

phrases.english: But since that is its normal way,
phrases.notes: "That" means swinging its tail, which the גמרא just called normal.

phrases.english: what was his question?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּאוֹרְחַיהּ, מַאי מִבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion of Step 9 (tail-swinging is normal) to question why Step 6 was asked at all.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the behavior is plainly normal, there is no doubt about the law, so the question has no point.

steps.title: The question was about excessive swinging
steps.stepSummary: The question was not about ordinary tail-swinging. It was about an animal swinging its tail more than usual.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was asking about extra, excessive swinging.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the question was about excessive tail-swinging, not normal swinging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normal swinging is clearly normal behavior. But when an animal swings much more than usual, it is not clear whether that still counts as its normal way. That doubt is what made the question worth asking.

phrases.english: He was asking about excessive swinging.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by narrowing the case of the question.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about ordinary tail-swinging, which is obviously normal.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question was about excessive swinging, where it is unclear whether it counts as normal behavior.

steps.title: רב עינא asks about an animal swinging its organ
steps.stepSummary: רב עינא asks about damage done when an animal swings its male organ. Is it like קרן, because its urge drives it, or different, because it has no intent to damage?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עינא asked: if an animal swung its organ and caused damage, what is the law? Do we say it is like goring, since with goring the animal's urge also overpowers it, so this is no different? Or perhaps with goring the animal means to do damage, while here it does not mean to do damage?
steps.whatsHappening: רב עינא raises a new question and lays out both sides. Is this kind of damage treated like קרן or not?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: in קרן the animal's inner urge overpowers it, and the same is true here, so it should be treated like קרן. Side two: what makes קרן special is that the animal intends to damage, and here there is no such intent. The question is what defines קרן: being driven by an urge, or intending to harm.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks a question he cannot settle

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows two possible ways to define what makes damage count as קרן: being overpowered by an urge, or intending to harm.

phrases.english: Rav Eina asked:
If it swung its male organ (and caused damage), what is the law?
Do we say it is just like goring:
with goring, isn't it that its urge overpowers it?
here too, it is no different;
or perhaps, with goring its intent is to damage,
while here its intent is not to damage?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב עֵינָא: כִּשְׁכְּשָׁה בְּאַמָּתָהּ מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, related question about unusual bodily motions, following the tail-swinging discussion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is damage from swinging the organ treated like קרן (urge-driven) or not (no intent to harm)?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רב עינא's question without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רב עינא's question with תיקו. No answer is found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side is proven. The question about swinging the organ stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: רב עינא's question of whether this is like קרן (urge) or not (no intent to harm) ends in תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of Step 12 without resolution.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The law of damage caused by an animal swinging its organ remains undecided.

steps.title: רב הונא limits the משנה about a string on a chicken
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about chickens. רב הונא says the half-damage ruling for a string on a chicken's leg applies only if the string got tied on by itself. If a person tied it, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: chickens are forewarned for walking in their normal way and breaking things, etc. רב הונא said: this was taught only where the string got tied on by itself. But if a person tied it, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new line of the משנה about chickens. רב הונא limits the ruling about a string tied to a chicken's leg.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules half damages when a string on a chicken's leg breaks something. רב הונא says this is only when the string got caught on its own. If a person tied it, that person is fully liable.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in a case of

phrases.english: Chickens are forewarned for walking in their normal way
and breaking, etc.
phrases.notes: The "etc." points to the rest of the משנה, which says the owner pays half if a string on the chicken's leg broke something.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
They taught this only where it got tied on by itself,
but if a person tied it, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּקְשַׁר מֵאֵלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next clause of the משנה about chickens.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Half damages apply only when the string got tied on by itself. If a person tied it, he is liable.

steps.title: If the string got tied by itself, who would pay?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who pays when the string got tied on by itself. If it is the string's owner, he was either careful (and helpless) or careless (and fully liable), so half-payment does not seem to fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it got tied on by itself, who is liable? If you say the owner of the string, what is the case? If he put it away, he could not help what happened! And if he did not put it away, he was negligent!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's case of a string tied on by itself. It asks who could be the one paying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first guess is the string's owner. But if he stored the string properly, he could not help what happened and should be exempt. If he left it lying around, he was negligent, like someone who tied it himself. Either way, the owner of the string does not fit the case.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who could not prevent what happened (exempt)
What is the case? What are the circumstances?

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides here are about the owner of the string, not the owner of the chicken. The גמרא is testing whether the string's owner could be the one who pays.

phrases.english: If it got tied on by itself, who is liable?
If you say the owner of the string,
what is the case?
If he put it away, he could not help it!
And if he did not put it away, he is negligent!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's case of a string tied on by itself (Step 14).
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's case of a string tied on by itself
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The string's owner is either helpless (exempt) or negligent (liable). Neither option fits the case.

steps.title: Maybe the chicken's owner pays, but a pit made by an animal is exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the chicken's owner is the one who pays. It rejects this, because the Torah says 'a man' opens a pit, not 'an ox', so an animal-made pit should be fully exempt, even from half.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, is the chicken's owner liable? Why is he exempt from full damage? Because the Torah says 'a man opens a pit', not an ox. Then he should be exempt from half damage too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new answer: the payer is the owner of the chicken. Right away it knocks this answer down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the chicken dragged the string into a spot where things trip on it, the chicken made a בור. The פסוק says 'כי יפתח איש בור', so only a person makes his owner liable for a pit, not an animal. That reasoning wipes out all payment, so it cannot explain why the משנה gives half.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If a man opens a pit', the פסוק about the damage category of בור
and not an ox making a pit; a pit made by an animal does not make its owner liable

phrases.english: Rather, is the owner of the chicken liable?
What is the reason he does not pay full damage?
Because it is written: "If a man opens a pit"
and not an ox opening a pit;
for half damage too,
"a man" opens a pit, and not an ox opens a pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 15 showed the string's owner cannot be the half-payer, so the גמרא tries the chicken's owner and rejects that too.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the chicken's owner pays half damage in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A pit created by an animal is exempt by the פסוק 'איש בור ולא שור בור'. That exemption covers all payment, so half damage has no basis.

steps.title: The משנה is about a chicken that flung the string
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new reading: the משנה is talking about a chicken that kicked or flung the string, so it is not a pit case at all. רב הונא's statement was not said on the משנה. It was a general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the משנה is a case where the chicken flung the string. And רב הונא's statement was said about a general case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes how it reads the משנה. It also moves רב הונא's rule away from the משנה, and the next step will spell that rule out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the chicken's own movement threw the string and caused the damage, the payment is the half-damage of indirect force from an animal, not a pit. That is why the משנה says half. רב הונא's distinction between 'tied by itself' and 'tied by a person' belongs to a different, general case.

keyTerms.meaning: where it actually flung or kicked it
it was said in general, not on this משנה

phrases.english: Rather, the משנה
is a case where it flung it.
phrases.notes: The chicken itself jerked the string so it hit something. It is not just lying there like a pit.

phrases.english: And when the statement of רב הונא was said,
it was said about a general case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Both possible payers in a pit case failed, so the גמרא reads the משנה as a non-pit case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case of the משנה and moving the אמורא's statement to a different case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה was a pit case, and רב הונא was explaining it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is a case of the chicken flinging the string, which pays half. רב הונא spoke about a separate, general case.

steps.title: רב הונא's rule about an ownerless string
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא's real statement: if an ownerless string got tied to a chicken by itself, no one is liable. If a person tied it, that person is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: About an ownerless string, רב הונא said: if it got tied on by itself, exempt. If a person tied it, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the exact case where רב הונא's rule was originally said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the string is הפקר, no string owner can be blamed. If it got tied on by chance, nobody is responsible. If a person tied it, he created the hazard, and he pays.

keyTerms.meaning: it got tied on by itself

phrases.english: Regarding an ownerless string,
רב הונא said:
if it got tied on by itself, exempt;
if a person tied it, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the 'general case' that step 17 said רב הונא was talking about.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With an ownerless string, no one pays if it got tied on by itself. The person who tied it pays.

steps.title: Under which damage category is he liable?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which category of damage makes the person who tied the string liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of what is he liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step. It wants to know which category of damage applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The string moves around with the chicken, so it does not look like a normal pit, which stays in one place. So which category of נזק fits?

keyTerms.meaning: because of what, under which category

phrases.english: Because of what is he liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the legal basis of רב הונא's 'liable'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which category of damage makes the person who tied the string liable

steps.title: It is a rolling pit
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח answers that it counts as his בור that rolls around at the feet of people and animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח said: because of his pit that rolls at the feet of people and animals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the person is liable under the category of בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A hazard does not have to stay still to count as a בור. An obstacle that a person set up, which moves around and trips people and animals, is still his pit. That is why the person who tied the string pays.

keyTerms.meaning: at the feet of people and animals

steps.whatToRemember: In a pit case the chicken's owner is exempt, because an animal cannot make a בור for its owner. The משנה's half damage is a case of the chicken flinging the string. A person who ties an ownerless string is liable under בור, as a rolling pit.

phrases.english: רב הונא בר מנוח said:
Because of his pit that rolls around
at the feet of people and the feet of animals.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ מִשּׁוּם בּוֹרוֹ הַמִּתְגַּלְגֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is liable under בור, because a moving obstacle he set up counts as his pit.

steps.title: משנה: The tooth is מועד for food that suits the animal
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: an animal is מועד, meaning its owner pays full, for eating fruits and vegetables. If it ate clothing or utensils, the owner pays half.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is the tooth מועד? To eat what is fit for it. An animal is מועד to eat fruits and vegetables. If it ate a garment or utensils, the owner pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about the damage category of שן, an animal eating things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal is expected to eat food that suits it, so its owner pays full damage for that. Eating clothes or utensils is unusual, so the owner pays only half.

keyTerms.meaning: tooth, the damage category of an animal eating
forewarned, the owner pays full damage
what is fit for it to eat

phrases.english: משנה: How is the tooth forewarned?
To eat what is fit for it.
The animal is forewarned
to eat fruits and vegetables.
If it ate a garment or utensils,
he pays half damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on שן after finishing the chicken-string discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Full payment for an animal eating food that suits it. Half payment for eating clothing or utensils.

steps.title: משנה: This applies only in the damaged person's property
steps.stepSummary: The משנה limits its rule: liability for eating applies in the property of the damaged person. In the public domain, the owner is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: When was this said? In the property of the damaged person. But in the public domain, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a limit on where the owner has to pay for eating damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שן is liable only in רשות הניזק. If the animal eats while walking in רשות הרבים, which is normal behavior there, the owner is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: when was this said, introduces a limit

steps.confusionAlert: The exemption in רשות הרבים is about שן, eating. Do not apply it to every type of damage.

phrases.english: In what case was this said?
In the property of the damaged person;
but in the public domain, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 21 to the damaged person's property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Payment for שן applies only in the damaged person's property. In the public domain, the owner is exempt.

steps.title: Even in the public domain, the owner pays for the benefit
steps.stepSummary: The משנה adds that even where the owner is exempt, he still pays for whatever benefit his animal got from eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the animal benefited from what it ate, the owner pays for the benefit it got.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its rule about eating in the public domain. The owner is exempt from the damage there, but he still pays for the benefit his animal got.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 22, the owner was exempt in the public domain. Now the משנה limits that exemption: he still pays for the value of what his animal enjoyed. He does not pay the full loss, only the benefit he received.

keyTerms.meaning: the value of the benefit it got

steps.confusionAlert: Paying 'what it benefited' is not the same as paying the damage. It is usually less, because the owner pays only for what his animal enjoyed, not for the full loss.

phrases.english: And if it benefited,
it pays for what it benefited.
phrases.notes: The animal 'pays' here, but it means the owner pays on its behalf.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the public-domain exemption from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the public domain, the owner pays for the benefit his animal got, though not for the full damage.

steps.title: How does paying for the benefit work?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks in which cases the owner pays only for the benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: In what case does the owner pay only for the benefit?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks a question to set up its next move. It is about to show exactly where the 'benefit only' rule applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line between 'public domain' and 'the damaged person's property' is not always clear. This question prepares a set of examples that draw that line.

phrases.english: How does it pay for what it benefited?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical cases of the rule in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which locations count as public (pay benefit only) and which count as the damaged person's property (pay full damage).

steps.title: The square and the store: where you pay benefit and where you pay damage
steps.stepSummary: Inside the open square or at a store's entrance, the owner pays the benefit. At the sides of the square or inside the store, he pays the full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the animal ate in the middle of the square, the owner pays for the benefit. If it ate from the sides of the square, he pays for the damage. If it ate from the entrance of a store, he pays for the benefit. If it ate from inside the store, he pays for the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers its question with two pairs of places. Places where people walk count as public, so the owner pays the benefit. Places off the walking path count like the damaged person's own property, so he pays the full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The middle of the square and a store's entrance are places animals normally pass through, so food left there is the food owner's own fault. The sides of the square and the inside of a store are not walking paths. An animal eating there is like eating in the damaged person's property.

keyTerms.meaning: the open square (in front of the stores)
the sides of the square, off the walking path

steps.whatToRemember: Public walking areas (middle of the square, store entrance): pay only the benefit. Areas off the path (sides of the square, inside the store): pay the full damage.

phrases.aramaic: אָכְלָה מִתּוֹךְ הָרְחָבָה – מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁנֶּהֱנֵית,
phrases.english: If it ate in the middle of the square, it pays for what it benefited;
from the sides of the square, it pays for what it damaged.
From the entrance of the store, it pays for what it benefited;
from inside the store, it pays for what it damaged.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָכְלָה מִתּוֹךְ הָרְחָבָה מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁנֶּהֱנֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24 with examples.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The middle of the square and the store entrance count as public (pay benefit). The sides of the square and inside the store count as the damaged person's property (pay full damage).

steps.title: A ברייתא: שן is מועד to eat what is fit for it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא: an animal that eats or drinks suitable food in the damaged person's yard, or a wild animal that kills and eats an animal there, pays full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: שן is considered מועד to eat what is fit for it. How so? If an animal entered the damaged person's yard and ate food fit for it or drank drinks fit for it, the owner pays full damage. Likewise, if a wild animal entered the damaged person's yard, tore apart an animal, and ate its meat, the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by bringing a ברייתא that defines שן. Eating or drinking what is natural for the animal is normal behavior, so the owner pays full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key idea is 'fit for it': eating that matches the animal's nature counts as שן and gets full payment. The wild animal case shows that killing and eating another animal is also שן, because for a predator, that is normal eating.

keyTerms.meaning: 'tooth': damage done by an animal eating
what is fit for it to eat

phrases.english: GEMARA. The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: הַשֵּׁן מוּעֶדֶת לֶאֱכוֹל אֶת הָרָאוּי לָהּ –
phrases.english: The tooth is מועד to eat what is fit for it.
How so? An animal that entered the damaged person's yard
and ate food fit for it
or drank drinks fit for it:
he pays full damage.
And likewise, a wild animal that entered the damaged person's yard
and tore apart an animal and ate the meat:
he pays full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַשֵּׁן מוּעֶדֶת לֶאֱכוֹל אֶת הָרָאוּי לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה's rule that eating is מועד (step 21).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating or drinking what is fit for the animal, including a predator eating prey, is שן and requires full payment.

steps.title: Less common foods still count as normal eating
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: a cow eating barley, a donkey eating vetch, a dog licking oil, or a pig eating meat all pay full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a cow that ate barley, a donkey that ate vetch, a dog that licked oil, or a pig that ate a piece of meat: the owners pay full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds cases where the animal ate something it does not usually eat. These still count as normal eating, so the owner pays full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These foods are not the animal's usual diet, but eating them is not strange behavior either. So they still fall under שן, not under unusual damage that pays only half. This sets up רב פפא's inference in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: vetch, a type of bean usually fed to cattle

phrases.english: And a cow that ate barley,
and a donkey that ate vetch,
and a dog that licked the oil,
and a pig that ate a piece of meat:
they pay full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the ברייתא's definition of 'fit for it' to less common foods.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Foods an animal eats less often still count as normal eating (שן) and require full payment.

steps.title: רב פפא: a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full damage
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא concludes from the ברייתא that anything an animal eats when pressed counts as eating, so a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Now that you have said that anything not usual for an animal, which it eats when pressed, still counts as eating, then a cat that ate dates or a donkey that ate fish: the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא takes the rule from the ברייתא and applies it to new cases. If unusual foods eaten under pressure still count as eating, then even a cat eating dates is שן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא showed that eating is not limited to an animal's usual diet. רב פפא pushes this further, to foods that are quite far from the animal's nature but that it will still eat when hungry. Since this is still eating, it is full-damage שן, not half-damage unusual behavior.
steps.whatToRemember: שן covers more than an animal's usual diet. Anything it will eat when pressed counts as eating, so the owner pays full damage.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
Now that you have said
that anything that is not its usual way,
but it eats it when pressed,
is called eating,
then this cat that ate dates,
and a donkey that ate fish:
he pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the ברייתא's cases in step 27 and applies it to new animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food an animal eats only when pressed still counts as eating (שן), so a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full damage.

steps.title: רב יהודה's ruling on the donkey, the bread and the basket
steps.stepSummary: A donkey ate bread and broke the basket. רב יהודה ruled full damage for the bread and half damage for the basket.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a donkey that ate bread and broke the basket it was in. רב יהודה made the owner pay full damage for the bread and half damage for the basket.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case and gives רב יהודה's ruling. One act of damage is split into two payments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating bread is treated as normal eating (שן), so it gets נזק שלם. Breaking the basket is treated as unusual damage, so it gets only חצי נזק. The next steps will ask why the two are treated differently.

phrases.english: There was a certain donkey that ate bread
and broke the basket,
Rav Yehuda obligated him to pay
full damage for the bread,
and half damage for the basket.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב פפא's rule about what counts as normal eating, the גמרא brings a practical case about eating plus extra damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bread eaten by a donkey: נזק שלם. Basket broken by it: חצי נזק.

steps.title: Why only half for the basket?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if eating bread is normal, breaking the basket to get it should also be normal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? If it is normal for a donkey to eat bread, it is also normal for it to break the basket to get at the bread!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the second half of רב יהודה's ruling. It thinks the basket should also be full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument: getting to the bread usually means pushing through the basket. So breaking the basket is part of the normal eating, and should be full damage like the bread.

keyTerms.meaning: its normal way, what it usually does

phrases.english: But why?
Since it is its normal way to eat bread,
it is also its normal way to break the basket!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the half-damage part of רב יהודה's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The חצי נזק for the basket.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Breaking the basket comes along with normal eating, so it should be normal damage and get נזק שלם.

steps.title: It ate first and broke the basket afterward
steps.stepSummary: The donkey broke the basket only after it finished eating, so the breaking was not part of eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: It ate the bread, and only afterward broke the basket.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by explaining the order of events. The basket was broken after the eating was done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the basket broke while getting to the bread, it would be part of eating and full damage. But breaking it after eating is extra, unusual damage, like קרן, so it is only חצי נזק.
steps.whatToRemember: Damage done while eating is part of eating. Damage done after eating is unusual and gets only חצי נזק.

phrases.english: It ate and then afterward broke it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The basket broke while the donkey was getting at the bread.
steps.terutzMaskana: The basket broke after the eating was over, so it is unusual damage.

steps.title: Is eating bread really normal? A ברייתא says half damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that charges only חצי נזק when an animal eats bread, meat or cooked food, suggesting bread is not normal food for a בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is bread really normal for it to eat? A contradiction: if it ate bread, meat or a cooked dish, the owner pays half damage. Isn't this talking about a domestic animal?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions the first half of רב יהודה's ruling, the full payment for the bread. It brings a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Half damage in the ברייתא means eating bread is treated as unusual. If the ברייתא is about a בהמה like a donkey, then eating bread is not normal for it, and רב יהודה should not have charged full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: and they pointed out a contradiction
a domestic animal, like a cow or donkey

phrases.english: But is bread its normal way?!
And they raised a contradiction:
If it ate bread, meat, or a cooked dish,
he pays half damage.
What, is it not talking about a domestic animal?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the bread part of רב יהודה's ruling and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's full payment for the bread.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives only חצי נזק for eating bread, which shows bread is not normal food for a בהמה.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about a wild animal
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about a חיה, which does not normally eat bread, not a בהמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about a wild animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is not talking about a donkey or a cow. It is talking about a wild animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a חיה, eating bread is unusual, so half damage makes sense. For a בהמה, bread is normal food, so רב יהודה's full payment stands.

phrases.english: No, it is about a wild animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction by changing which animal the ברייתא means.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the case to a different kind of animal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is about a בהמה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a חיה, for which bread is unusual.

steps.title: But wild animals normally eat meat
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא is about a חיה, it should not charge half damage for meat, since wild animals normally eat meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A wild animal? Eating meat is its normal way!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. The ברייתא also lists meat, and meat is normal food for a wild animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If meat is normal for a חיה, eating it should be full damage. So the ברייתא's half damage for meat does not fit a חיה.

phrases.english: A wild animal? Meat is its normal way!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer that the ברייתא is about a חיה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is about a חיה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists meat as unusual food, but meat is normal food for a wild animal.

steps.title: The meat was roasted
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means roasted meat, which a wild animal does not normally eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about roasted meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the meat in the ברייתא was cooked by roasting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wild animals normally eat raw meat, not roasted meat. So eating roasted meat is unusual for a חיה, and half damage fits.

phrases.english: It is roasted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by defining what kind of meat the ברייתא means.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means roasted meat, which is unusual for a חיה.

steps.title: Another answer: the ברייתא is about a deer
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the ברייתא is about a deer, which does not eat meat or bread at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: it is about a deer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to answer the meat problem. The wild animal in the ברייתא is a deer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A deer is a wild animal that does not eat meat, so even raw meat is unusual for it. That way, every food in the ברייתא is unusual, and half damage fits.

phrases.english: Or if you want, say: it is about a deer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the meat challenge, instead of roasted meat.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the case to a specific animal
steps.terutzMaskana: The חיה is a deer, which does not normally eat meat or bread.

steps.title: Another answer: a domestic animal eating off the table
steps.stepSummary: A third answer: the ברייתא really is about a בהמה, but one that ate food off a table.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: really it is about a domestic animal, and it ate from a table.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer to the original contradiction. It keeps the ברייתא about a בהמה but changes where it ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bread is normal food for a בהמה, but eating it from a table is not normal. That unusual way of eating is why the ברייתא gives only חצי נזק, so it does not argue with רב יהודה.
steps.whatToRemember: Eating bread is normal for a בהמה, so it pays נזק שלם. The ברייתא's חצי נזק is either about a חיה (roasted meat or a deer) or about a בהמה eating off a table.

phrases.english: Or if you want, say:
really it is about a domestic animal, and it ate from a table.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the original contradiction (step 32) and answers it a different way, keeping the ברייתא about a בהמה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (where the animal ate)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא means a בהמה eating bread in a normal way.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means a בהמה eating off a table, which is unusual.
